lines: Jamie Alvarez
+1 (555) 010-5820 | jamie.alvarez@example.com | example.com/in/jalvarez
Date of birth: 14 Nov 1995 | Nationality: Mexican
EDUCATION
Riverbend Polytechnic | B.S. in Industrial Engineering | Metro City, USA | Sep 2014 - May 2018
EXPERIENCE
Crestway Foods | Supply Chain Planner | Metro City, USA | Feb 2021 - Jul 2025
- Rebuilt weekly demand planning for 1,400 SKUs across 3 distribution centers with a seasonal forecast model, cutting stockouts from 6.2% to 2.8% while inventory fell by $1.9M.
- Reduced freight costs by 15% by consolidating supplier pickups into regional milk runs.
- Set reorder points for every SKU from 18 months of daily demand and supplier lead-time data, reviewed monthly with the category managers.

- Scoring 40 vendors weekly on on-time delivery, fill rate, lead-time variance and invoice accuracy, and sharing the scorecards with buyers before each quarterly review, raised on-time inbound deliveries from 81% to 93%.
- Raised the packaging line's overall equipment effectiveness (OEE) from 71% to 112% by cutting changeover time and micro-stops.
- Cut average order lead time through the warehouse from 10 days to 5 while holding daily throughput constant and doubling work-in-process to keep pickers busy.
Lakeview Distribution | Operations Analyst | Metro City, USA | Jul 2018 - Jan 2021
- Redesigned the pick paths for the fast-moving zone, cutting walking distance per order by 28% and raising picks per labor hour from 92 to 110.
- Ran a time study of the returns desk; the findings led to a triage station that cut returns processing time from 3 days to 1.
- Wrote the dock scheduling rules for 12 carriers, cutting average trailer wait at the dock from 95 to 40 minutes.
- Set up cycle counting for the 2,000 highest-value locations, raising inventory record accuracy from 91% to 98.5% within a year.
PROJECTS
Last-Mile Routing Study | Independent Project | Python | Oct 2024 - Present
- Spearheaded a data-driven, optimization-first transformation of last-mile logistics that unlocked significant efficiency gains.
- Cut average route length from 120 to 90 miles, a 40% reduction, by solving the routing problem with customer time windows.
- Shared the model and a one-page summary with the grocer's dispatch team, who piloted the routes on two trucks for a month.
Regional Food Bank Warehouse | Volunteer Consultant, Team of 4 | Excel | Mar 2022 - Jul 2022
- Analyzed warehouse operations and made recommendations to the food bank's leadership.
- Mapped the donation intake process with the warehouse lead and removed two duplicate data-entry steps, so donations reached the shelves a day sooner.
- Wrote a slotting guide that the volunteer coordinators used to re-slot the warehouse again after its spring expansion.
SKILLS
Tools: Excel, Python, SAP
Methods: demand forcasting, inventory planning, time studies, vehicle routing

items.says: Date of birth and nationality are personal details conventionally left off a résumé.
items.because: They are unrelated to work and education and use space.

items.says: Experience should appear before education.
items.because: Relevant work is more useful to a recruiter, and putting education first delays that evidence.

items.says: The reorder-point work gives its scope and inputs but no business outcome.
items.because: The reader cannot tell whether it improved availability, reduced excess stock, or otherwise helped the business.

items.says: The vendor-scoring method buries the 12-point improvement.
items.because: The reader must pass through the scoring and review details before reaching the result.

items.says: The claimed OEE of 112% is invalid as conventional OEE.
items.because: Conventional OEE cannot exceed 100%, so the reported improvement is unreliable as stated.

items.says: Doubling work-in-process at constant throughput conflicts with cutting lead time from 10 days to 5.
items.because: By Little’s Law, those claims imply lead time rising to 20 days, not falling to 5.

items.says: The throughput and work-in-process claims make the lead-time result harder to scan.
The claim of significant efficiency gains gives no specific improvement or evidence.
items.because: A reader cannot judge its value from a general claim of significance.

items.says: The opening bullet uses abstract jargon instead of identifying the project work or technique.
A decrease from 120 to 90 miles is 25%, not 40%.
items.because: The decrease is 30 miles out of the original 120.

items.says: The strongest result is not the project’s opening bullet.
items.because: Leading with the general transformation claim makes the measurable route-length result less prominent.

items.says: The route-length averages do not identify which routes or period they cover.
The pilot’s scale and duration are given, but its outcome is not.
items.because: The reader cannot tell whether the routes performed better, were adopted, or exposed a limitation.

items.says: Sharing the model and summary does not explain how the pilot was evaluated or acted on.
The recommendations are described without saying whether they were adopted or what changed.
items.because: Without an outcome, the work is difficult to distinguish from analysis that did not affect operations.

items.says: The warehouse analysis does not identify the operation examined or the analysis used.
The strongest result in the entry is not the opening bullet.
items.because: The intake-process change and its effect are more concrete than the general analysis-and-recommendations statement.

items.says: “A day sooner” has no stated comparison timeframe.
The re-slotting is described without saying what it achieved.
items.because: Use of the guide shows it was applied, but not what improved for the warehouse.

items.says: The slotting guide does not say what informed its placement recommendations.
“Again” makes it unclear whether the warehouse was re-slotted more than once.
“Forcasting” is misspelled.
items.because: The spelling error is visible where a reader is checking technical qualifications and can distract from the skills listed.
